transcript:
Header:
- Date/Time: 2025-10-21 15:00 UTC
- Duration: 60 minutes
- Attendees: Sam Rivera (Redwood AE), Dr. Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood Product); Jared Klein (Apex Head of ML Infra), Priya Malhotra (Apex SRE), Felix Gordon (Apex ML Eng)

Auto-generated summary: Medium quality transcript. Some ASR substitutions expected (K V vs KV, Kubernetes vs Kubernetis, etc).

00:00:00 Sam Rivera: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda — dig into the KV cache eviction Apex reported, look at logs Sam shared earlier, repro steps, and next steps. Maya will lead the deep technical part.
00:00:18 Jared Klein: Thanks Sam, yeah we've been seeing frequent kv cache evictions when sessions hit ~120k tokens, we're seeing paging to host spike and latency variance climbs.
00:00:32 Dr. Maya Chen: Okay awesome. Can you remind us of the model config — sequence length, batch sizes, quantization?
00:00:40 Felix Gordon: Sure, on prod we're running a 2.7B open model, 8-bit quantized (per our pipeline), typical request is a 16k prompt plus dynamic history, batching at 16 across our requests. We saw evictions at around 90-130k total context.
00:00:58 Priya Malhotra: The weird part is the eviction isn't correlated to instantaneous QPS, it looks more to do with working set and prefix reuse patterns, like when we have a handful of long-lived sessions with long prefixes.
00:01:15 Dr. Maya Chen: That maps to the KV cache heuristics — Redwood runtime keeps token KV per attention layer in GPU memory and uses LRU-ish eviction plus a paging path to host when total KV exceeds configured limit. Were you using the default cache size?
00:01:28 Jared Klein: We used the default cache cap in the Dedicated config. I think it's 20GB per shard in our setup, but not 100% on memory accounting because we also have model and activation reservations.
00:01:41 Liam O'Connor: Quick note: default cap can be influenced by sequence length distribution and compiled kernel choices; longer sequences increase KV density.
00:01:52 Felix Gordon: What we observed — when we hit eviction, requests that previously completed in ~120ms jump to 350-700ms and some hit a 2s tail.
00:02:05 Dr. Maya Chen: That's consistent with paging back from host. When the runtime evicts KV to host, reaccessing that prefix causes a host->device copy. If multiple layers page, you get multi-stage copies and large latency spikes.
00:02:22 Jared Klein: Is eviction policy purely LRU? It seems like it sometimes evicts prefixes that are actively reused.
00:02:30 Dr. Maya Chen: It's LRU augmented with working-set heuristics; but in some access patterns with many interleaved sessions, the heuristics mis-prioritize. Also, prefix reuse across sessions can be missed if keys are stored per-session rather than hashed by canonical prompt id.
00:02:49 Priya Malhotra: Ah — we do a lot of prefix reuse across customer sessions — same system prompt, minor user variations. We expected reuse to be leveraged, but maybe our session isolation prevents that.
00:03:05 Sam Rivera: Can you describe how you're pinning sessions? Are you binding to Dedicated shards or using dynamic routing?
00:03:13 Jared Klein: Dynamic routing — requests are routed to free capacity; that likely breaks local KV reuse because sessions land on different shards.
00:03:22 Dr. Maya Chen: Right — dynamic routing trades throughput utilization for local cache affinity. For long-context workloads with heavy prefix reuse, pinning sessions to shards or using affinity routing helps reduce evictions.
00:03:35 Felix Gordon: If we pin, won't we lose some autoscale flexibility? We need predictable throughput but also want to utilize capacity.
00:03:45 Liam O'Connor: There are hybrid strategies — soft-affinity where the router prefers previous host but can overflow; or sticky pools for long-lived sessions. Reducing inter-shard churn reduces KV copies and eviction churn.
00:03:58 Jared Klein: Okay, good. Regarding paging — we saw logs showing host_copy_in and host_copy_out spikes. Maya, you had a repro?
00:04:08 Dr. Maya Chen: Yes, Sam shared a set of perf logs. I looked at the timeline: when the largest session expands its prefix, the runtime evicts older, less recently used keys, then on the next request the same session needs the evicted keys and triggers host->device transfers. The host paging path is single-threaded in our current kernel, so that exacerbates tail latencies.
00:04:33 Priya Malhotra: Single-threaded? That's surprising. Could we at least make the host copy multi-threaded?
00:04:40 Dr. Maya Chen: We have a roadmap item to parallelize host-device copy for large KV pages, but it depends on kernel and pinned memory strategies. Short term, we can tweak eviction thresholds and prefetch heuristics.
00:04:52 Felix Gordon: What about batching? We're batching at 16. Could batching be increasing effective working set and causing evictions?
00:05:00 Dr. Maya Chen: Yes — larger batches multiply the KV footprint because multiple requests' contexts are resident. There's a threshold where batching reduces per-token cost but increases peak memory leading to evictions. We should look at batch-size vs latency slope.
00:05:15 Jared Klein: We can try lowering batch to 8 for long-context sessions and keep 16 for short ones. But routing split becomes more complex.
00:05:23 Sam Rivera: Another lever is quantization — you mentioned 8-bit. That reduces KV size but can increase compute cost or change kernel choices. Any chance quantization is changing kernel selection such that KV layout is less cache-friendly?
00:05:36 Felix Gordon: We used a post-training 8-bit quantization. Model was compiled with fallback kernels for some ops. Not sure about KV layout changes.
00:05:45 Dr. Maya Chen: Quantization reduces memory but can change alignment and packing of KV tensors; in some cases alignment leads to slightly larger per-token KV. Also, some quantized kernels don't support fused KV layouts, forcing separate buffers. We should check compiled kernel report.
00:06:02 Liam O'Connor: We'll pull the compile report; Sam, can you share the kernel selection log?
00:06:07 Sam Rivera: Yep, I'll include compile_and_kernel_report.txt in the repo I'll share.
00:06:12 Jared Klein: On the replay side — we noticed eviction often follows a spike in concurrent long sessions after a release. Could we detect bursty arrival and temporarily raise KV cap to avoid eviction?
00:06:25 Dr. Maya Chen: There is an autoscaling knob and a burst-capacity policy. You could configure the Dedicated config to allow short-lived overcommit for KV or increase reservation during scheduled releases. But that increases cost.
00:06:38 Priya Malhotra: Cost is acceptable if it avoids 2s tails for user-facing flows. We'll evaluate tradeoffs.
00:06:46 Felix Gordon: Are there visibility tools to pinpoint which prefixes are being evicted? The logs show host_copy_out but not the prefix ids.
00:06:55 Dr. Maya Chen: Current logs show session_id and layer index, but not canonical prompt hash. We can enable an optional flag in the runtime to log prompt_hash->evicted mapping for debugging. It's verbose, so we'd do it for repro only.
00:07:09 Jared Klein: Let's enable that for a short run.
00:07:12 Sam Rivera: I'll toggle debug_eviction=true and send instructions.
00:07:15 Dr. Maya Chen: Also, there are two strategies to reduce eviction impact: 1) prefix canonicalization across sessions so identical system prompts share KV; 2) smarter prefetch on predicted reuse. Both require changes — canonicalization needs upstream consistency on prompt ids, and prefetch needs predictive policy.
00:07:34 Priya Malhotra: For canonicalization, our frontend can compute a canonical prompt id for the system prompt + template, and include prompt_hash in the request. Does Redwood support prompt_hash reuse?
00:07:44 Dr. Maya Chen: We have a prompt_key field in the routing proto; if you pass that, the runtime uses it to namespace/lookup shared KV. That would be perfect. I can send the proto example.
00:07:54 Felix Gordon: Great. That should cut a lot of redundant KV.
00:07:58 Jared Klein: About prefetching — do you prefetch from host when session grows predictively?
00:08:05 Dr. Maya Chen: We have an LRU-based hint prefetch for linear growth, but it doesn't handle random-access or interleaved patterns well. We can add a warmup hook for newly-activated sessions to fetch likely prefixes.
00:08:17 Liam O'Connor: We should also evaluate whether switching to sticky-pinning for long-lived sessions reduces total host traffic more than increasing underutilization. We'll model it in the optimizer.
00:08:27 Sam Rivera: Can we walk through the repro steps? Jared, you had a test harness?
00:08:33 Jared Klein: Yes. Steps: 1) create N long sessions (N=50) with a 16k prefix each, 2) interleave short bursts of new sessions to create churn, 3) measure eviction events and host copy times. We have harness code in Apex's perf repo, will attach link.
00:08:48 Dr. Maya Chen: Perfect. For our repro we'll run on a staging Dedicated with the same shard count. We'll enable debug eviction mappings and collect nvprof / device memory timelines and host copy traces.
00:09:01 Priya Malhotra: Timeline wise, we can provision the staging cluster by Thursday if Redwood provides the runbook.
00:09:07 Sam Rivera: I'll share the runbook and the kernel reports.
00:09:10 Dr. Maya Chen: For mitigation short-term: 1) pass prompt_hash to enable prefix reuse, 2) lower batch size for long sessions, 3) enable soft-affinity routing for long-lived sessions, 4) enable debug eviction logging for repro. Medium-term: parallel host-device copy, smarter prefetch, kernel-level fused KV layouts for quantized models.
00:09:34 Felix Gordon: Sounds good. Any thoughts on VPC/on-prem implications? If we deploy on-prem, will host paging differ because of network-mounted memory?
00:09:44 Dr. Maya Chen: On-prem VPC usually has lower latency between host and device but if you're using NVLink vs PCIe it changes bandwidth. Also, for air-gapped setups we can configure larger local ephemeral storage to avoid paging to remote hosts. We should validate on your target hardware.
00:09:59 Jared Klein: We'll document our target on-prem spec.
00:10:03 Sam Rivera: Quick Q from sales side — any concerns about SOC2 or audit logs if we enable debug mapping?
00:10:09 Dr. Maya Chen: Debug mapping logs only include prompt_hash (not raw text) and session ids. We can mask PII and keep logs within the same retention and ACL controls. We'll coordinate with security.
00:10:20 Priya Malhotra: Good.
00:10:22 Liam O'Connor: Okay, let's surface the concrete next steps so we can close this call.
00:10:28 Sam Rivera: Recap and next steps — Sam will share repro repo, kernel reports, and enable debug flag instructions (due 2025-10-23). Apex will provision staging and run repro with logs (due 2025-10-28). Redwood to run a follow-up with quantization and runtime team during week of 2025-11-03.
00:10:45 Jared Klein: Agreed. Thanks folks.
00:10:48 Dr. Maya Chen: Thanks, we'll also prepare a short doc on canonicalization and example proto for prompt_key.
00:10:55 Sam Rivera: I'll send meeting notes and links. Attaching: link to shared perf spreadsheet (https://redwood.app/sheets/apex-kv-repro), repo: git://apex/perf/harness (Apex internal), kernel report placeholder: compile_and_kernel_report.txt.
00:11:10 Felix Gordon: One last quick question — when you say prefix reuse, do you mean reuse across sessions or within a session? We do both.
00:11:18 Dr. Maya Chen: Both, but cross-session reuse has the biggest win if you can canonicalize. Within-session reuse is already leveraged by the runtime unless evicted.
00:11:27 Priya Malhotra: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in Slack and schedule the next session after we have repro logs.
00:11:33 Sam Rivera: Great. Bye all.

End of transcript.

Notes:
- Mentioned artifacts: compile_and_kernel_report.txt, repro harness link, perf spreadsheet
- Suggested flags: debug_eviction=true, prompt_key field in routing proto
- Suggested mitigations: soft-affinity, lower batch for long sessions, prompt canonicalization, parallel host copy (mid-term)
